stem: A team needs Claude to call an internal inventory service exposed as a REST API. They want the capability to be reusable across several Claude applications and maintained independently of any one app. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Hard-code the inventory logic into each application's system prompt.
options.explanation: Hard-coding logic into prompts is neither reusable nor maintainable.

options.text: Build an MCP server that exposes the inventory operations as tools so multiple Claude applications can connect to it.
options.explanation: Correct. An MCP server exposes reusable tools that multiple Claude applications can share and that can be maintained independently.

options.text: Paste the current inventory data into the context window on every request.
options.explanation: Pasting data gives no live access and wastes context.

options.text: Rely on a built-in tool, since built-in tools can reach any internal REST API.
options.explanation: Built-in tools do not automatically reach arbitrary internal APIs.

stem: A broadcast research team pastes the same twelve-step procedure for building a pregame stat package into Claude Code every week. All the data already lives in the repository, so no new system access is needed. They want the procedure available on demand without loading it into every session. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Build an MCP server that exposes each of the twelve steps as its own tool.
options.explanation: MCP adds access to external systems. Nothing external is involved here, so a server adds code and deployment work without giving Claude anything it lacks.

options.text: Paste the procedure into CLAUDE.md so that it is present in every session.
options.explanation: CLAUDE.md loads in full every session, which is the opposite of the on-demand requirement. A procedure needed only sometimes belongs in a Skill.

options.text: Capture the procedure as a Skill that loads when the task comes up or is invoked.
options.explanation: Correct. Skills package reusable workflows. Only their name and description load up front, and the body loads when the task matches or a user invokes it.

options.text: Define a custom tool whose description field holds the full twelve-step procedure.
options.explanation: A tool description is meant to explain a callable capability, not to carry a playbook. It would also be sent with every request that includes the tool.

stem: A sports-news app built on the Claude API must answer questions about trades announced in the last hour, using public web sources with citations. An engineer plans to write and maintain a custom scraping tool for this. What should the team do instead?

options.text: Enable the built-in web search tool instead of building and maintaining a scraper.
options.explanation: Correct. The web search server tool gives Claude current web content with cited sources, so a generic need like this does not justify custom code.

options.text: Build the scraper anyway, because server tools can only search Anthropic-hosted data.
options.explanation: The web search tool searches the public web. Building a custom tool for a job a built-in already does just adds code to maintain.

options.text: Upload a Skill with a scraping script, since API Skills can reach the open internet.
options.explanation: Skills on the API run in a code-execution container with no network access, so a scraping script there cannot fetch anything.

options.text: Load yesterday's headlines into the system prompt and let Claude infer today's news.
options.explanation: Old headlines cannot reveal trades announced in the last hour. The requirement is live access, which pasted context cannot provide.

stem: An insurance company uploads a custom Skill that formats claim summaries, and references its skill_id in the container parameter of Messages API requests. The requests do not include any other tools, and the Skill is never applied. What is the most likely fix?

options.text: Upload the same Skill on claude.ai so that it syncs to the API workspace.
options.explanation: Custom Skills do not sync between surfaces, and the API copy is already uploaded. Another upload elsewhere changes nothing here.

options.text: Set disable-model-invocation to false in the Skill's frontmatter.
options.explanation: That is a Claude Code frontmatter field, and false is already its default. It does not affect how the API runs Skills.

options.text: Copy the Skill's instructions into the system prompt of each request.
options.explanation: This might approximate the behavior, but it gives up progressive disclosure and any bundled scripts, and it does not fix the missing prerequisite.

options.text: Add the code execution tool to the request so the Skill has a container.
options.explanation: Correct. Skills on the API run inside the code execution tool's container, so requests that use Skills must include that tool.

stem: A fantasy platform's single back-end service needs Claude to call calc_projected_points, a function that already lives in the same codebase. No other application will use it, and the team already runs its own tool-use loop. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Stand up a separate MCP server so the function can be deployed on its own.
options.explanation: MCP pays off when several apps share a capability or another team owns it. With one app and one owner, it adds a service to run for no benefit.

options.text: Define a custom tool with a JSON Schema and run it in the existing loop.
options.explanation: Correct. One app needing one specific capability that it owns is the classic case for a custom tool executed in the application's own loop.

options.text: Write a Skill that explains the formula so Claude computes points itself.
options.explanation: Skills add know-how, not access to your code. Having Claude reproduce the calculation risks drift from the real function the service already has.

options.text: Use the code execution tool to import the function from the repository.
options.explanation: The code execution container is a sandbox on Anthropic's side. It cannot import modules from your private codebase.

stem: A retailer's data-platform team owns a sales warehouse that three different Claude applications must query. Analysts also report that Claude writes poor SQL because it doesn't know the team's table naming and join conventions. Which design addresses both problems?

options.text: Three custom tools, one per application, each with the conventions in its prompt.
options.explanation: Duplicating the integration in three apps gives up a single, independently maintained implementation, and the conventions drift across three prompts.

options.text: A Skill holding the warehouse credentials and query scripts for all three apps.
options.explanation: Credentials never belong in a Skill, and a Skill does not give live access to a private warehouse. It is the right home for know-how, not for the connection.

options.text: An MCP server for warehouse access, plus a Skill documenting schema and query patterns.
options.explanation: Correct. MCP gives every app one shared, team-owned connection, and a Skill teaches Claude how to use it well. Combining the two is the recommended pattern.

options.text: A long CLAUDE.md listing every table, which each application loads at startup.
options.explanation: CLAUDE.md is a Claude Code memory file, not a way to connect API apps to a warehouse. It also loads in full every session, whether or not SQL is needed.

stem: A stadium-operations team uses Claude Code in a repository that can run database migrations. Leadership requires that Claude never runs the migration command against the production database, with no exceptions. Someone suggests writing a safe-migrations Skill. Which extension actually meets the requirement?

options.text: A PreToolUse hook that blocks the production migration command before it runs.
options.explanation: Correct. Hooks fire deterministically on every matching event, and a PreToolUse hook can block the call. A rule that must always hold belongs in a hook, not in instructions.

options.text: A Skill whose description says it applies to every database migration task.
options.explanation: A Skill is instructions that Claude interprets and might not load or follow. It is guidance, not enforcement.

options.text: A rule written in capital letters at the very top of the project's CLAUDE.md.
options.explanation: CLAUDE.md content is context Claude reads, so it is a request rather than a guarantee, however it is formatted.

options.text: A dedicated migrations subagent with its own system prompt forbidding production.
options.explanation: A subagent isolates context, but its system prompt is still an instruction. Nothing outside the model stops the command.

stem: A league-operations assistant on the Messages API sends 60 custom tool definitions with every request, although a typical request uses three or four. Input-token costs are rising and Claude increasingly picks the wrong tool. The team needs all 60 tools to stay available. Which change best addresses both problems?

options.text: Merge the 60 tools into one generic tool that accepts free-form instructions.
options.explanation: A catch-all tool throws away the schemas that make tool calls precise and moves the selection problem into your own code.

options.text: Move the tool definitions into a Skill so they load only when it triggers.
options.explanation: Skills package instructions and scripts. They don't hold API tool definitions for your own tool-use loop, so this doesn't reduce what each request sends.

options.text: Set temperature to 0 so that Claude chooses among the tools consistently.
options.explanation: Current models reject non-default sampling parameters, and sampling settings would not shrink the tool definitions sent on every request.

options.text: Keep a small core set loaded and defer the rest so tool search loads them on demand.
options.explanation: Correct. With the tool search tool, deferred definitions load only when needed. That cuts context use and keeps selection accurate while all 60 tools stay available.

stem: A team's publish-depth-chart Skill runs a script that pushes roster changes to the club's public website. Last week Claude triggered it on its own when a coach only asked to review the depth chart. The team wants to keep the Skill but make sure it runs only when a person deliberately starts it. What should they change?

options.text: Make the Skill's description vaguer so that it matches fewer requests.
options.explanation: A vaguer description makes matching less predictable, not safe. Claude could still invoke the Skill automatically.

options.text: Set disable-model-invocation: true in the Skill's frontmatter.
options.explanation: Correct. This field stops Claude from loading the Skill automatically, so it runs only when someone invokes it by name. The docs recommend it for workflows with side effects.

options.text: Move the publish script into CLAUDE.md so Claude always sees the risk.
options.explanation: Putting the procedure into always-loaded context makes it more prominent and does nothing to stop automatic use.

options.text: Add the publish script to allowed-tools in the Skill's frontmatter.
options.explanation: allowed-tools pre-approves tools while the Skill is active. That removes a safety prompt instead of adding one.

stem: A media company's Skill works well in Claude Code from the repository's .claude/skills folder. The team expects it to appear automatically in their Claude API application, and it doesn't. After they upload it to the API, its script, which calls an external stats service, fails. Which explanation covers both problems?

options.text: Skills sync between surfaces only after an admin turns on organization-wide sharing.
options.explanation: There is no sharing switch that syncs Skills. Custom Skills are uploaded or installed separately on each surface, and this does not explain the failing network call.

options.text: The Skill's name must carry a workspace prefix before other surfaces can discover it.
options.explanation: No naming prefix controls availability across surfaces, and a name change would not let the script reach an external service.

options.text: Custom Skills don't sync across surfaces, and API Skills run without network access.
options.explanation: Correct. Each surface needs its own upload or install, and Skills on the API run in a code-execution container that cannot make external calls.

options.text: The Skill's metadata exceeds the token budget, so other surfaces skip loading it.
options.explanation: Metadata size does not explain why the Skill is missing from the API before upload, and it does not explain a failed outbound request.

stem: A platform team is extending Claude Code for 40 engineers. They need to add a large library of internal reference guides and connections to six internal services, while keeping the context each session uses at startup small. Which two choices meet both goals? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Package the reference guides as Skills, which load only their descriptions at startup.
options.explanation: Correct. Skills use progressive disclosure: name and description load up front, and the body and bundled files load only when needed.

options.text: Connect the services as MCP servers and rely on tool search to load schemas on demand.
options.explanation: Correct. In Claude Code, tool search is on by default, so MCP tool definitions load when needed instead of all at startup.

options.text: Move all the reference guides into CLAUDE.md, which is cached between sessions.
options.explanation: CLAUDE.md loads in full into every session, so a large library there inflates startup context. That is the reverse of the goal.

options.text: Ask engineers to paste the relevant guide into the prompt whenever they need it.
options.explanation: This keeps startup context small but is manual and inconsistent. It does not package the library or connect any service.

options.text: Turn the reference guides into hooks, which add nothing to context without output.
options.explanation: Hooks run code at lifecycle events. They don't give Claude reference knowledge to apply, so they cannot replace the guides.

stem: A stadium's gate-operations team found a third-party Skill and a companion MCP server on a public marketplace that would automate ticket scanning reports. Both include scripts that will run with the team's access. Which two precautions are most appropriate before adopting them? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Audit the bundled scripts and any network calls they make before installing.
options.explanation: Correct. The docs advise reviewing every file in a Skill for unexpected network calls or file access that don't match its stated purpose.

options.text: Install them only from a source the team trusts, treating them like software.
options.explanation: Correct. Skills and MCP servers run code with your access, so they deserve the same trust decision as any software you install.

options.text: Rely on the Skill's description field to confirm that it behaves safely.
options.explanation: The description is written by the author to help Claude match tasks. It is not evidence about what the scripts actually do.

options.text: Put the ticketing API key in SKILL.md so the scripts can authenticate.
options.explanation: Secrets in a Skill file are visible to the model and to anyone with the file. Credentials belong in the environment or a secrets manager.

options.text: Run the session in bypassPermissions so the scripts never stall on prompts.
options.explanation: Removing permission prompts for untrusted code widens the damage it could do. That increases risk instead of reducing it.

stem: A team installs a Skill for formatting weekly injury reports. Its `SKILL.md` body is detailed and correct, but its `description` reads only "Helpers." Claude never uses the Skill unless someone types its name. Which change best fits?

options.text: Move the whole Skill body into CLAUDE.md so Claude always sees it
options.explanation: This loads the full procedure into every session and gives up the Skill's on-demand loading.

options.text: Make the body longer and more detailed so Claude recognizes when it applies
options.explanation: Until the Skill triggers, Claude sees only the name and description. The body plays no part in the decision.

options.text: Rewrite the description to say what the Skill does and when to use it
options.explanation: Correct. The description is what Claude sees at startup and uses to decide whether to load the Skill, so it must name the task and the situations it fits.

options.text: Set `disable-model-invocation: true` so the Skill is picked up more reliably
options.explanation: That setting does the opposite: only a person can trigger the Skill.

stem: A team uploads a custom Skill to the Claude API. Its bundled script calls the club's live stats REST API, and the calls always fail with network errors, although the same script works on a developer's laptop. Requests include the code execution tool. Which design best fits?

options.text: Raise the script's network timeout, since the container is slower than a laptop
options.explanation: The container has no network access, so no timeout will let the call through.

options.text: Expose the stats API via a tool or MCP server; keep the Skill for know-how
options.explanation: Correct. API Skills run in the code-execution container without network access. New access belongs in a tool or MCP server; the Skill can still teach Claude how to use it.

options.text: Put the stats API key in `SKILL.md` so the script can authenticate from the container
options.explanation: Authentication isn't the problem, and secrets don't belong in Skill files.

options.text: Remove the code execution tool so the Skill runs in the application's own process
options.explanation: API Skills need the code execution tool to run at all. Removing it disables the Skill.

stem: A roster-validation Skill describes a long, fully deterministic salary-cap check as 300 lines of step-by-step prose in `SKILL.md`. It costs a lot of context whenever the Skill triggers, and Claude applies the steps slightly differently each time. Which change best fits?

options.text: Split the prose across several Skills so each one loads less text
options.explanation: The same logic still enters context as prose, and Claude still applies it by interpretation.

options.text: Move the check into CLAUDE.md so it is always in context and applied consistently
options.explanation: This costs context in every session, and prose stays prose wherever it lives.

options.text: Add "follow every step exactly" at the top of the prose
options.explanation: Emphasis doesn't make interpreted prose deterministic or shorter.

options.text: Bundle the check as a script the Skill runs, so only its output enters context
options.explanation: Correct. A script runs the logic the same way every time, and with progressive disclosure only its output reaches context, not its code.

stem: A club's ticket-allocation system is a 20-year-old Windows desktop application with no API. Staff re-key allocation requests from emails into its forms. The team wants Claude to automate the data entry. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Build an MCP server that calls the application's REST API.
options.explanation: The application has no API for an MCP server to wrap.

options.text: Use the computer use tool against the application in a sandboxed VM with minimal privileges, and have a human confirm each submission before it is committed.
options.explanation: Correct. Computer use lets Claude operate graphical applications through screenshots and mouse and keyboard actions, which suits a system with no API. Sandboxing and a confirmation step limit the risk.

options.text: Use the web fetch tool to submit the forms.
options.explanation: Web fetch retrieves web content. It can't operate a desktop application.

options.text: Write a Skill describing the data-entry steps.
options.explanation: A Skill provides instructions, but on its own it gives Claude no way to act on the desktop app.

stem: A platform team is deciding how to extend Claude for three needs: (1) a fixed weekly reporting procedure the team follows, with its templates; (2) live access to a vendor's ticketing system that several Claude apps must share; (3) a small pricing function that exists only inside one backend service. Which THREE mappings fit best? (Select THREE.)

options.text: The ticketing integration written separately as a custom tool inside each app.
options.explanation: Duplicating the integration in every app is what MCP is meant to avoid.

options.text: The reporting procedure pasted into every app's system prompt.
options.explanation: This costs context on every request and must be maintained in several places. A Skill loads on demand.

options.text: Access to the vendor's ticketing system as an MCP server.
options.explanation: Correct. MCP gives a reusable integration that several clients and apps can connect to.

options.text: The pricing function as a custom tool defined in that one service's API requests.
options.explanation: Correct. A function used by a single application fits a client tool defined right where it lives.

options.text: The weekly reporting procedure and templates as a Skill.
options.explanation: Correct. Skills package procedures and reference files and load them only when relevant.

options.text: The pricing function exposed as a public MCP server.
options.explanation: A function that only one service uses doesn't need its own server and transport.

stem: A fantasy app built on the Claude API lets users upload a season of weekly stats as a CSV file and ask for trends, correlations and a chart. The team plans to build and host its own Python sandbox as a custom tool so Claude can run analysis code. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Enable the code execution server tool, and pass the CSV in through the Files API.
options.explanation: Correct. Code execution is a built-in server tool: Claude runs Python in an Anthropic-hosted sandbox with data libraries preinstalled, reads files uploaded through the Files API, and can save charts you download afterwards. Nothing needs to be built or hosted.

options.text: Paste the CSV into the prompt and ask Claude to work out the statistics in its answer.
options.explanation: Without code to run, Claude computes correlations by reasoning over raw numbers, which is less reliable and spends context on the whole file. It also can't produce a chart file.

options.text: Build an MCP server that wraps the sandbox, so other Claude apps could reuse it later.
options.explanation: Nothing in the scenario calls for reuse across apps, and the team would still have to build and secure its own sandbox. A built-in tool already does the job.

options.text: Write a Skill that describes the analysis steps, and run it without any execution tool.
options.explanation: A Skill adds know-how, not compute. On the API, Skills themselves run inside the code execution container, so a Skill alone can't run analysis code.

stem: A rules assistant on the Claude API must answer questions about rulebook PDFs and press releases on the league's own websites. Users paste the links into the chat, and answers must cite the passages they rely on. An engineer proposes a custom download_url tool that the app would run. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Use the web search tool alone, since it returns the complete text of any page it finds.
options.explanation: Web search finds pages for a query and returns search results; it isn't meant for reading the full content of a specific URL the user supplied.

options.text: Build the download_url tool, because built-in server tools cannot read PDF documents.
options.explanation: The premise is false. The web fetch tool retrieves both web pages and PDFs, so a custom download tool only adds code to build and maintain.

options.text: Enable the web fetch server tool with citations on, and limit it with allowed_domains.
options.explanation: Correct. Web fetch is a built-in server tool that reads the full content of URLs present in the conversation, including PDFs. Citations are optional and can be enabled, and allowed_domains keeps fetching to the league's sites.

options.text: Ask users to paste each document's text instead of a link, so nothing needs fetching.
options.explanation: This pushes the work onto users and loses PDF structure and page-level citations. A built-in tool already handles the links they paste.

stem: In Claude Code, a developer asks Claude to find every place the depth-chart service reads injury data. Claude reads about 60 files to answer, and afterwards the main session is so full of file contents that it loses track of the refactor in progress. The team runs investigations like this several times a week. Which extension best fits?

options.text: A subagent, which does the reading in its own context and sends back only a summary.
options.explanation: Correct. Subagents run in an isolated context window. They can read dozens of files, and the main conversation receives only their findings, so the refactor's context stays intact.

options.text: A Skill that describes how to search the codebase, loaded whenever the topic comes up.
options.explanation: A Skill's content loads into the main conversation, and the files it leads Claude to read land there too. It adds know-how but doesn't isolate context.

options.text: A longer CLAUDE.md section that lists where each service reads its data from.
options.explanation: CLAUDE.md loads in full every session, so this costs context all the time, goes stale as code changes, and doesn't keep investigation output out of the main session.

options.text: An MCP server that exposes the repository's files as tools for Claude to call.
options.explanation: Claude Code already has built-in file tools, and results from MCP tools also land in the main context. The problem is where the work happens, not access.

stem: A team is setting up Claude Code for a stats repository. They have three needs: (1) Claude must always know the build and test commands; (2) a 25-step season-rollover procedure that they run once a year; (3) the formatter must run after every file Claude edits, with no exceptions. Which choices fit best? (Select THREE.)

options.text: Put the build and test commands in CLAUDE.md, which loads in every session.
options.explanation: Correct. CLAUDE.md is for facts Claude should always know, such as build commands and conventions.

options.text: Put the season-rollover procedure in CLAUDE.md so that it is always available.
options.explanation: CLAUDE.md loads in full every session, so a yearly 25-step procedure would cost context on every request. Procedures needed only sometimes belong in a Skill.

options.text: Capture the season-rollover procedure as a Skill that is invoked when needed.
options.explanation: Correct. A Skill loads only its description until it is used, then brings in the full procedure. It can also be started on demand with its slash command.

options.text: Add a CLAUDE.md rule telling Claude to run the formatter after each edit.
options.explanation: An instruction is a request that Claude interprets, not a guarantee. "No exceptions" calls for something that runs automatically.

options.text: Package the build commands as an MCP server that Claude can query for them.
options.explanation: MCP connects Claude to external services. A few commands Claude should always know need no server, only always-loaded context.

options.text: Add a PostToolUse hook that runs the formatter after each file edit.
options.explanation: Correct. Hooks fire on lifecycle events without Claude deciding, so the formatter runs after every matching edit.
